direction: Warm, conversational and curious. One connected explanation, with natural breaths. No trailer delivery or forced excitement.

scenes.hook: What if a microscope knew when to look?
scenes.premise: Imaging light can alter cells. One high-dose near-ultraviolet study found eighty percent fewer divisions. That's why we built Peekaboo, the software that chooses when to take the next microscopy image.
scenes.demo: Both sides replay the same controlled experiment. Fixed timing keeps capturing. Peekaboo waits through quieter periods, then captures more often when acquired images show a shape change. Watch the divisions.
scenes.result: In this selected example, thirty-two Peekaboo images cover all four divisions; forty fixed captures cover one. That is twenty percent fewer exposures, assuming equal light per image.
scenes.causality: Peekaboo decides only from acquired images. It tracks shape, chooses the next capture time and stays within its budget. Hidden frames remain separate for evaluation.
scenes.gaussians: Each nucleus becomes a Gaussian with position, brightness, and shape. Inspired by recent four-dimensional cell-reconstruction research, our simplified model shortens gaps when acquired shapes elongate.
scenes.frontier: Our GPU renderer uses NVIDIA's cue-tile Rust library, first released in April. The CPU fits shapes and chooses capture times; the GPU renders the models.
scenes.benchmark: With ten thousand Gaussians, warmed GPU rendering was twelve point seven times faster than the CPU reference. That is the rendering call, not overall app speed.
scenes.difficulty: We checked GPU output against the CPU and excluded startup costs. Smaller workloads still use the CPU when GPU overhead dominates.
scenes.limits: Sudden divisions can be missed. Our separate real-microscopy benchmark did not improve coverage over fixed timing, so biological validation remains ahead.
scenes.close: Next, we'll validate the approach on real microscopes. Peekaboo: see more, illuminate less.
